docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
nbdctools

This Python package provides tooling for working with tabulated data released by the NIH Brain Development Cohorts (NBDC) Data Hub for the ABCD and HBCD studies.

The package is designed to help researchers and data analysts create integrated datasets from tabulated data files. Building on the R package NBDCtools, it provides a thin wrapper around the core R functionality, and a simplified pure-Python alternative for users who prefer to work in Python without an R installation.

Citation

Citing nbdctools

Developers Le Zhang Author, maintainer Janosch Linkersdörfer Author

docs.title: Citation
docs.text:
If you use this package for your research, please kindly cite the following paper:

Zhang, L., Das, B., Celhay, O., Smith, C. J., Ziemer, L. R., Dale, A. M., & Linkersdörfer, J. (2026). NBDC Data Tools: Building Analysis-ready Datasets From ABCD and HBCD Releases in R and Python. bioRxiv. https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.02.763757

• Fixed download_metadata(type="dds"), which failed with HTTP 413 because r-universe can no longer convert lst_dds for download. It now saves the metadata file from the NBDCtoolsData source package as lst_<type>.rda, and load_metadata reads .rda as well as .rds files.
  • Fixed create_dataset_py join semantics so that results no longer depend on the order variables and tables are listed in, and so that a coarser-grained value reaches every finer row it applies to. Previously a participant-level variable could land on a separate all-null row instead of on that participant's sessions.
  • Fixed create_dataset_py additional selections (vars_add / tables_add): each is now joined on its own identifier columns. Previously they were joined to each other first, which wrote nulls into identifier columns and let one additional table silently blank out another's values.
  • vars_add / tables_add no longer change the row set. An additional table finer than the main selection now keeps one value per row, leaves the finer identifier columns out of the result, and warns.
  • An additional table with duplicate identifier rows now raises ValueError instead of silently multiplying rows.
  • Documented the join and grain semantics for create_dataset_py, including that they match NBDCtools::join_tabulated() with finer_add = "first".
  • Re-ran the benchmark page on ABCD 7.0 with NBDCtools 1.1.2 and this release's code.
  • Added the package citation: Zhang, L., Das, B., Celhay, O., Smith, C. J., Ziemer, L. R., Dale, A. M., & Linkersdörfer, J. (2026). NBDC Data Tools: Building Analysis-ready Datasets From ABCD and HBCD Releases in R and Python. bioRxiv. https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.02.763757. It is shown in the import message, the README, and the documentation home page, and GitHub's "Cite this repository" reads it from the new CITATION.cff.
  • Corrected wording and links throughout the documentation. The quickstart no longer claims that create_dataset_py skips type coercion; it applies the variable types from the data dictionary.
• No changes from 1.0.2. This version was released before the changes listed under 1.0.4 were merged.
• Updated docs with better instructions.

• Initial Python package release.
  • Added R-backed create_dataset wrapper behavior.
  • Added pure-Python workflow with create_dataset_py.
  • Added metadata helpers: download_metadata and load_metadata.
  • Added MkDocs documentation site and GitHub Pages deployment workflow.

docs.title: Install from PyPI
docs.text: pip install nbdctools

docs.title: R packages
docs.text:
If you want to use the R-backed create_dataset wrapper, which has full parity with the R create_dataset behavior, you need:

  • System R available on PATH
  • R packages: NBDCtools, NBDCtoolsData, and arrow (for the default polars_sink return mode)

docs.title: R Library Discovery (R_LIBS_USER)
docs.text:
If R packages were installed with renv and are not discovered by rpy2, export R_LIBS_USER:

export R_LIBS_USER=/path/to/your/renv/library
python your_script.py

For one-off commands:

R_LIBS_USER=/path/to/your/renv/library python your_script.py

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
There are two options for using nbdctools to create datasets:

  • The R-backed create_dataset wrapper, which has full parity with the R create_dataset behavior and forwards all extra keyword arguments to NBDCtools::create_dataset.
  • The pure-Python create_dataset_py, which joins tabulated files using the data dictionary and applies its variable types, but does not cover further processing steps such as labeling or missingness handling.

Read the R wrapper guide and the pure-Python guide for more details on each workflow.

docs.title: R-backed wrapper
docs.text:
from nbdctools import NBDCtoolsRError, create_dataset

try:
    df = create_dataset(
        dir_data="/path/to/tabulated/data",
        study="abcd",
        vars=["var1", "var2", "var3"],
        tables=["table1", "table2"],
        release="latest",
    )
    print(df.shape)
except NBDCtoolsRError as exc:
    print(exc)
    print(exc.r_message)

docs.title: Pure-Python
docs.text:
from nbdctools import create_dataset_py, load_metadata, download_metadata

# Download the metadata once; it is saved as lst_dds.rda
download_metadata(type="dds")
# Load the downloaded file into the session
dds = load_metadata("lst_dds.rda")
# Choose the study and release of interest
dd = dds["abcd"]["7.0"]

df = create_dataset_py(
    dir_data="/path/to/tabulated/data",
    dd=dd,
    tables=["table1", "table2"],
    vars=["var1", "var2", "var3"],
)

print(df.shape)

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text:
Everything below is importable directly from nbdctools:

from nbdctools import (
    NBDCtoolsRError,
    create_dataset,
    create_dataset_py,
    download_metadata,
    load_metadata,
)

docs.title: nbdctools.create_dataset(dir_data, study, *, return_mode='polars_sink', **kwargs)
docs.text:
Python wrapper around NBDCtools::create_dataset.

This function forwards all R arguments to the backend implementation and only validates Python-specific return mode behavior.

docs.title: nbdctools.create_dataset_py(dir_data, dd, vars=None, tables=None, vars_add=None, tables_add=None, format='parquet', categ_to_factor=True, progress=True)
docs.text:
Pure Python dataset joiner based on a data-dictionary dataframe.

Tables are joined on the identifier columns they declare in the data dictionary, which differ by table: participant-level tables are identified by participant_id alone, session-level tables by participant_id and session_id, and run-level tables also by run_id. A value from a coarser table is repeated on every finer row it applies to, so a participant-level variable such as birth data appears on every session and every run of that participant. The result does not depend on the order variables or tables are listed in, and holds one row per distinct combination of identifier columns.

vars/tables are the main selection and determine the row set. vars_add/tables_add annotate those rows and never add, remove or duplicate one. A variable named in both is taken from the main selection.

If an additional table is more finely grained than everything in the main selection (for example a session-level vars_add on top of a participant-level selection), its values cannot all be attached without adding rows. One value per row is kept and the surplus is dropped: the value kept is the first by the additional table's own identifier columns, i.e. the earliest session or the first run, and the finer identifier columns are not added to the result. This always emits a UserWarning. To keep every value, select those variables via vars/tables instead, so the finer grain becomes part of the row set.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: dd Data dictionary dataframe. Accepts a Polars or pandas DataFrame and must include columns: name, table_name, and identifier_columns.

docs.title: Raises
docs.text: ValueError If required metadata columns are missing, if requested variables or tables are absent from dd, if two selections share no identifier column, or if an additional table has more than one row per identifier combination. FileNotFoundError If a required data file is not present in dir_data.

docs.title: nbdctools.download_metadata(type='dds', path=None, progress=True)
docs.text:
Download a metadata file from the NBDCtoolsData source package on r-universe.

The file is saved as a gzip-compressed .rda (by default lst_<type>.rda), which load_metadata reads.

docs.title: nbdctools.load_metadata(path, progress=True)
docs.text: Load a metadata file (.rda or .rds) into nested dicts and Polars DataFrames.

docs.title: Benchmark Scope
docs.text:
The benchmark compares these methods:

  • R:create_dataset_direct: Calling NBDCtools::create_dataset in a fresh Rscript subprocess. The dataset stays in R and only its dimensions cross the process boundary, so this measures assembly in R with no conversion to Python. It is the baseline the other R-backed rows are compared against.
  • create_dataset:polars_sink: The create_dataset wrapper with return_mode="polars_sink", which writes the dataset to a temporary file via an R Arrow sink and reads it back into Python as a Polars DataFrame.
  • create_dataset:polars: The wrapper with return_mode="polars", which converts the R dataset to a Polars DataFrame directly through rpy2.
  • create_dataset:pd: The wrapper with return_mode="pd", which converts the R dataset to a pandas DataFrame directly through rpy2.
  • create_dataset:pd_sink: The wrapper with return_mode="pd_sink", which writes the dataset to a temporary file via an R Arrow sink and reads it back into Python as a pandas DataFrame.
  • create_dataset_py: The pure Python create_dataset_py, which builds the dataset from tabulated files and metadata without involving R.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
Every timed run executes in its own operating system process, so no R session state is reused between runs. This is not a detail: NBDCtoolsData lazy-loads the data dictionary on first use and caches it for the life of the session, and R pays further first-call costs for byte-compilation and method dispatch. Together that is roughly 4.9 seconds per R session on this workload. Timing repeated calls inside one embedded R session therefore flatters every method that can reuse it, and penalises the subprocess baseline, which cannot.

All R-backed methods are called with identical arguments (add_labels=False, ignore_version_mismatch=True, bypass_ram_check=True), so the only thing that differs between them is the conversion path. Labels are off because create_dataset_py cannot apply them, which keeps it comparable to the rest.

What is timed: the call that produces the dataset, including the metadata resolution it performs. For create_dataset_py that includes load_metadata, because the R methods pay the equivalent cost inside create_dataset.

What is not timed: Python interpreter startup. The subprocess baseline additionally carries about 0.13s of R interpreter startup inside its timed region, which is inherent to how that method works.

Three timed runs per method, preceded by one untimed run that is discarded. That run warms the operating system page cache for the data files, which is shared between processes; the R session it creates is not, which is the point.

docs.title: Dataset
docs.text:
ABCD release 7.0, Parquet format. The selection below produces a dataset of 139,095 rows × 825 columns, and every method produced exactly that shape.

TABLES = [
    "sdev_p_vt",
    "covid_p_qtn",
    "mh_y_ksads__bpd",
    "mh_y_sup",
    "fc_y_vs",
    "nc_y_nihtb",
    "ph_y_bld",
    "ph_y_phs",
]

VARS = [
    "ab_g_dyn__design_site",
    "ab_g_dyn__cohort_grade",
    "ab_g_stc__cohort_dob",
]

VARS_ADD = [
    "ab_g_stc__design_id__fam",
    "ab_g_stc__cohort_ethn",
    "ab_g_stc__cohort_sex",
    "ab_g_stc__cohort_acsps",
    "ab_g_dyn__visit_type",
    "ab_g_dyn__visit_age",
    "ab_g_dyn__design_id__school",
    "ab_g_dyn__design_mr__model",
    "ab_g_stc__design_id__fam__gen",
]

docs.title: Results
docs.text: Method Median (s) Min (s) R:create_dataset_direct 15.58 15.46 create_dataset:polars_sink 15.96 15.89 create_dataset:polars 172.50 172.49 create_dataset:pd 28.60 28.48 create_dataset:pd_sink 15.53 15.30 create_dataset_py 3.74 3.71

docs.title: What this shows
docs.text:
• The sink modes are effectively free. polars_sink and pd_sink land within a few tenths of the R baseline, which does no conversion at all. Assembly inside R dominates, and the Arrow round-trip costs almost nothing on top of it. If you want the data in Python, a sink mode is the way.
  • return_mode="polars" is the one to avoid, at roughly 11× the sink modes. Converting an R data frame to Polars through rpy2 column by column is the dominant cost of that path, not the assembly.
  • return_mode="pd" sits in between, about 1.8× the sink modes. rpy2's pandas conversion is far better than its Polars conversion, but still much worse than going through Arrow.
  • create_dataset_py is about 4.2× faster than the R-backed paths, and roughly 2.8s of its 3.74s is load_metadata parsing the 14 MB metadata file rather than the join itself. It does less, though: it performs the join and type casting only, with no labels, value transformations, missingness handling or filtering. See pure Python for the full comparison of what the two paths cover.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Performance can vary with data location, file format, software versions, and runtime environment.
  • These figures were measured on 2026-10-31 with the grain fix present on both sides: NBDCtools 1.1.2 (which includes the join fix) with NBDCtoolsData 6.0.0, and create_dataset_py after the equivalent fix. On the same selection the two implementations return identical values in all 823 non-identifier columns across all 139,095 rows.
  • load_metadata read a 14 MB lst_dds.rds saved from NBDCtoolsData 6.0.0 with saveRDS().
  • Figures published before 2026-10-08 are not comparable and were wrong in two ways. They were recorded on ABCD 6.1 against a pre-fix create_dataset_py that silently dropped roughly 41% of the participant-level values it reported. They also timed the four create_dataset:* rows in one warm, reused R session while the baseline started cold every time, which made the sink modes look faster than the R call they wrap.

docs.title: Metadata Workflow
docs.text: nbdctools provides metadata helpers for download and local loading.

docs.title: Download Metadata
docs.text:
from nbdctools import download_metadata

dds_path = download_metadata(type="dds", path="./metadata", progress=True)
levels_path = download_metadata(type="levels", path="./metadata", progress=True)
sessions_path = download_metadata(type="sessions", path="./metadata", progress=True)

Supported type values:

  • dds
  • levels
  • sessions

The legacy alias seesions is accepted for compatibility.

Each call downloads the NBDCtoolsData source package from r-universe and saves one metadata file, by default lst_<type>.rda.

docs.title: Load Metadata
docs.text:
from nbdctools import load_metadata

dds = load_metadata("./metadata/lst_dds.rda", progress=False)
dd = dds["abcd"]["6.1"]

load_metadata converts rds2py payloads into nested Python structures and Polars DataFrames where applicable.

load_metadata also reads .rds files, for example one saved in R with saveRDS(NBDCtoolsData::lst_dds, "lst_dds.rds").

Currently there are only abcd and hbcd studies in the metadata, and to find the release of interest one can inspect the keys of the nested dictionaries. For example, dds["abcd"].keys() will show all available releases for the ABCD study.

docs.title: Pure Python
docs.text: create_dataset_py builds joined datasets directly from tabulated files and metadata, without an R installation. It covers the join step only: type coercion from the data dictionary is applied, but labelling, missingness handling and the other post-processing steps of the R wrapper are not.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
The dd data dictionary must include:

  • name
  • table_name
  • identifier_columns

Input file formats supported by format:

  • parquet
  • tsv

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from nbdctools import create_dataset_py, load_metadata

dds = load_metadata("/path/to/lst_dds.rda", progress=False)
dd = dds["abcd"]["7.0"]

df = create_dataset_py(
    dir_data="/path/to/tabulated/data",
    dd=dd,
    tables=["table1", "table2"],
    tables_add=["table3"],
    vars=["var1", "var2", "var3"],
    vars_add=["var4"],
    format="parquet",
    categ_to_factor=True,
    progress=False,
)

docs.title: Join semantics
docs.text:
Tables are joined on the identifier columns they declare in the data dictionary. Three levels are in use, and they nest:

Grain identifier_columns Example participant participant_id demographics, birth data session participant_id \| session_id most assessments run participant_id \| session_id \| run_id some HBCD instruments

A value from a coarser table is repeated on every finer row it applies to, so a participant-level variable appears on every session and every run of that participant. The result holds one row per distinct combination of identifier columns, and does not depend on the order you list variables or tables in.

docs.title: Main and additional selections
docs.text:
• vars / tables are the main selection and determine the row set. Every row present in any selected table appears in the result.
  • vars_add / tables_add annotate those rows. They never add, remove or duplicate a row.
  • A variable named in both is taken from the main selection.

docs.title: When an additional table is finer than the main selection
docs.text:
A session-level vars_add on top of a participant-level selection, or a run-level one on top of a session-level selection, has more values than there are rows to put them on. Because the additional selection must not change the row set, one value per row is kept and the rest are dropped:

  • The kept value is the first by the additional table's own identifier columns — the earliest session, or the first run. The choice never depends on row order within the file.
  • The finer identifier columns are not added to the result, so the output does not look as though it were at the finer grain.
  • A UserWarning names the tables, the finer identifier columns, and how many values were dropped.

To keep every value, request those variables through vars/tables instead, which puts the finer grain into the row set.

These semantics match NBDCtools::join_tabulated() in the R package called with finer_add = "first", so the two implementations agree on the same inputs. Note that the R default, finer_add = "error", raises an error in this case instead.

docs.title: Behavior notes
docs.text:
• At least one of vars or tables must be provided.
  • Missing metadata columns raise ValueError.
  • Missing table files raise FileNotFoundError.
  • An additional table with more than one row per identifier combination raises ValueError, rather than silently multiplying rows.
  • Type casting is applied from metadata (type_data and optional type_level).

docs.title: R wrapper (create_dataset)
docs.text: The R wrapper function create_dataset provides a convenient interface for Python users to create datasets with exactly the same functionality as the R version. It runs R in the backend to leverage its data manipulation capabilities, while providing a Pythonic interface for ease of use. Therefore, an R installation and the R packages are required. See the installation guide for details on setting up the R environment and dependencies.

docs.title: Use the R wrapper
docs.text:
from nbdctools import create_dataset
# Example usage
create_dataset(
    dir_data="/path/to/tabulated/data",
    study="abcd",
    vars=["var1", "var2", "var3"],
    tables=["table1", "table2"],
    release="latest",
)

create_dataset accepts all the same arguments as the R version and forwards them to NBDCtools::create_dataset. All arguments must be passed by name; positional arguments are not supported.

docs.title: Return Modes
docs.text:
create_dataset supports four return modes.

create_dataset(..., return_mode="polars_sink")  # default
Mode Output Conversion Path Requirements polars_sink (default) Polars DataFrame R Arrow sink -> Feather -> Polars R arrow polars Polars DataFrame Direct rpy2 conversion R + rpy2 pd pandas DataFrame Direct rpy2 conversion Python pandas pd_sink pandas DataFrame R Arrow sink -> Feather -> pandas R arrow, Python pandas, Python pyarrow

docs.title: Practical Guidance
docs.text:
• Use polars_sink (the default) for the fastest path to a Polars DataFrame.
  • Use polars only when sink dependencies are unavailable (see the tradeoffs below).
  • Use pd or pd_sink only when downstream code requires pandas.
  • Sink modes fail fast when required dependencies are not available.

Read the benchmark results guide for performance comparisons of these modes. It is highly recommended to use *_sink modes for large datasets due to their superior performance.

docs.title: Tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Sink modes write large temporary files, which can be a concern when storage space is limited or storage I/O is slow. In such cases, direct rpy2 conversion modes may be more suitable despite their higher memory usage and slower performance.
  • If storage is a concern, consider pd mode. pandas may be slower than Polars in downstream processing, but its rpy2 conversion is more memory efficient and much faster than polars mode. You can convert the pandas DataFrame to Polars afterwards if needed, which is generally faster than direct rpy2 conversion to Polars.
  • Use polars mode only as a last resort, when sink dependencies are unavailable and pandas is not an option. This mode has the worst performance and highest memory usage due to the inefficiency of rpy2 conversion to Polars, and it is not recommended for large datasets.

docs.title: NBDCtoolsRError
docs.text: When calling create_dataset, R-side failures are wrapped as NBDCtoolsRError. Inspect exc.r_message to see the original R error.

docs.title: Missing R packages
docs.text:
If create_dataset fails to find R packages, verify these are installed in your R environment:

  • NBDCtools
  • NBDCtoolsData
  • arrow (required for sink modes)

docs.title: R library path issues
docs.text: If R packages are not found via rpy2, export R_LIBS_USER before starting Python. See R library discovery.

docs.title: Pure-Python metadata/file issues
docs.text:
• Missing metadata columns in dd raise ValueError.
  • Missing tabulated files raise FileNotFoundError.
  • No shared identifier columns between join groups raises ValueError.

docs.title: "Additional variables ... are more finely grained"
docs.text:
create_dataset_py emits this UserWarning when a table in vars_add/tables_add is at a finer grain than anything in vars/tables — for example a session-level variable added to a participant-level selection. The additional selection is not allowed to change the row set, so only the first value per row is kept and the warning reports how many were dropped.

Move those variables into vars/tables if you need all of their values. See join semantics.

docs.title: "Duplicate rows for ... in ..."
docs.text: A table used in vars_add/tables_add has more than one row per identifier combination, which would multiply the rows of your dataset. This usually means the data file does not match the grain its identifier_columns declare. Check the file, or request the variables through vars/tables instead.
